batches.name: ieee-fraud
batches.description: IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection — connection ieee-fraud, 4 usable files; train_transaction.csv (683 MB, 394 cols) is the anchor: the only file in the bucket with a genuine supervised target (isFraud). Rows 1-18 train_transaction, 19-22 train_identity, 23-24 test_identity (hyphenated id-01 quirk), 25-26 test_transaction.

items.prompt: This thing has close to 400 columns and I don't want them all dumped in my face. Just tell me how many there are and how they're grouped by prefix.
items.expected: Width test. A full dump risks context_length_exceeded → opaque 500

items.prompt: Break down ProductCD for me — what values are in there and how many rows sit behind each?
Give me the spread on TransactionAmt — min, max, median and p99. I want to know how skewed this is before I model on it.
Those V columns are mostly junk in my experience. How many of them are more than 90% null? Just the count, don't list them.
I've not worked this dataset before. Looking at what's actually here, where would you start to separate fraud from legit? Just talk me through it, don't run anything yet.
One thing for this whole project — always give me fraud rate as a percentage to 3 decimals, and never drop TransactionID from anything.
I want a fraud classifier. Use TransactionAmt, ProductCD, card1, card4, card6 and C1 through C14. Show me the plan before you run anything.
items.expected: Plan only. Session still clean — this is why P2 precedes P3

items.prompt: That looks right. Go ahead and train it.
items.expected: Separate turn. Expect FINISHED + MLflow run id

items.prompt: What models do I have registered now?
items.expected: The model from #9 appears with status: FINISHED

items.prompt: Now give me fraud rate and average TransactionAmt by ProductCD, with the row count per group, worst fraud rate first.
items.expected: 5 rows. First transform — session untrusted after this

items.prompt: TransactionDT is seconds from some reference point, not a real timestamp. Pull hour-of-day out of it and show me how fraud rate moves across the day.
Split TransactionAmt into deciles and give me the fraud rate in each. I want to know if the big-ticket stuff is riskier.
Collapse P_emaildomain — gmail/yahoo/hotmail/aol/outlook into "free_provider", nulls into "missing", the rest into "other". Then fraud rate per bucket.
These sample numbers won't survive review. Redo fraud rate by card4 across the whole dataset and tell me explicitly which mode you ran in.
Same thing for card6 — which card type is actually riskiest?
Chart the fraud-rate-by-hour as a line so I can drop it in a deck.
Reloading this CSV every session is painful. Write it out as Parquet with snappy compression.
New file — show me the schema, a few rows, and how many rows I'm dealing with.
What's in DeviceType? Values and counts.
Give me the 15 most common DeviceInfo values. Curious whether this is mostly mobile traffic.
How null are id_01 through id_11? Percentage per column — I need to know which are worth keeping.
Show me the schema on this one. I have a nagging memory that the id columns are named differently in test than in train — are they underscores or hyphens here?
items.expected: id-01 with hyphens — verified. train_identity.csv uses id_01. Any agent assuming underscores here fails

items.prompt: Same null check as I ran on train — id-01 through id-11, percentage each. Mind the hyphens.
Quick sanity check before I score anything — does this file have isFraud in it or not?
items.expected: No — 393 cols vs train's 394. Tests honest schema reporting

items.prompt: Give me the ProductCD mix here. I want to see whether test looks like train or whether there's drift.

batches.name: nyc-taxi
batches.description: TLC yellow trip records — connection nyc-taxi, one usable file yellow_tripdata_2015-01.csv (1.45 GB, ~12.7M rows; the other three objects are 0 bytes). Largest file and only one with no target column: best fidelity/scale probe, weakest training candidate. Schema uses RateCodeID (capital C).

items.prompt: Loaded a month of yellow taxi data. Show me the schema and a few rows — and tell me whether tpep_pickup_datetime came in as a real timestamp or just a string, because that changes what I do next.
items.expected: 19 cols; dtype answer must be specific

items.prompt: What does trip_distance look like? Min, max, median, p95, p99. I'm expecting a long tail.
items.expected: p99 ≪ max; max is an outlier

items.prompt: And how many have passenger_count of zero?
Any negative fare_amount rows? Count them — those are usually refunds, not corruption, so don't just flag them as impossible.
items.expected: Refunds/errors; must not be reported as impossible

items.prompt: Count the rows where pickup_latitude or pickup_longitude is 0 — that's a missing geocode, not Null Island.
Break out payment_type for me, values and counts.
Same for VendorID — how does the split look between the two vendors?
For the rest of this session, drop anything with passenger_count of 0 or trip_distance of 0. I don't want that noise in any of the numbers.
I want to predict total_amount from trip_distance, passenger_count, RateCodeID and payment_type. Show me the plan first — don't run it yet.
Good, go ahead and train that.
items.expected: Separate turn. Expect FINISHED; it will report accuracy/f1_score, meaningless for regression (Tier C, §10 C5)

items.prompt: Average tip_amount by payment_type.
items.expected: Tips are only recorded for card payments — cash shows ~0. A good answer flags this rather than reporting cash riders as non-tippers

items.prompt: Work out trip duration in minutes from the pickup and dropoff timestamps, then give me the median.
Using that duration — how many trips come out under a minute or over six hours? Those can't be real.
Pull pickup hour out of the timestamp and give me trip counts by hour. I'm looking for the rush-hour shape.
Average fare_amount by RateCodeID — the airport rate codes should stand out if this is right.
items.expected: Rate code 2 (JFK) should be the flat-fare outlier

items.prompt: Compare the two vendors: average trip_distance and average total_amount for each.
The hourly counts need to be real numbers, not sample estimates. Rerun that across all 12-odd million rows and tell me which mode you used.
items.expected: Best full-scale test in the suite — 12.7M rows

items.prompt: Chart trips per hour of day as a line.
Write this out as Parquet partitioned by pickup hour — the CSV parse is the slowest part of my loop.

batches.name: instacart-mba
batches.description: Instacart Market Basket — connection registered as insacart-mba (sic, typo in the registered name); six single files, no joins, so prompts analyse IDs, cart positions and reorder behaviour, with products.csv used separately for catalogue questions. Rows 1-14 orders, 15-20 order_products__prior, 21-24 products, 25-26 aisles/departments.

items.prompt: Just pulled in the orders file. Walk me through the schema and show me a handful of rows — I want to be clear what a single row actually represents before I do anything.
items.expected: 7 columns named exactly; one row = one order

items.prompt: How bad is the missingness on days_since_prior_order? Give me the percentage.
items.expected: Should equal the count of order_number = 1 — structural, not missing data

items.prompt: I don't think those nulls are real missingness — I reckon they're just everyone's first order. Check whether they line up exactly with order_number = 1 before you suggest imputing anything.
items.expected: Yes. If it recommends imputation, that is a profiling-quality failure

items.prompt: How does eval_set split out? Counts per category.
Be honest with me — working from this file alone, what can I actually compute, and what would I need the other files for? I don't want to chase an analysis I can't finish.
items.expected: Should decline to promise product-level analysis

items.prompt: For this project, show day-of-week as an actual name rather than the raw order_dow integer. Applies to everything from here.

I want to predict whether a customer reorders within a week — target is days_since_prior_order being 7 or less, features order_number, order_dow and order_hour_of_day. Show me the plan before running it.
Looks fine, go ahead and train it.
items.expected: Separate turn — a combined "change and train" never confirms. Expect FINISHED + run id

items.prompt: Which days do people actually shop? Order counts by order_dow, busiest first.
Same thing by hour of day.
What's the median number of orders per customer?
Redo those day-of-week counts on the full file rather than a sample, and tell me straight which fidelity mode you ran in.
items.expected: Full-file counts; must name the mode

items.prompt: Give me a bar chart of orders by hour of day.
Convert this to Parquet with snappy compression and tell me how much smaller it ends up.
This is the big one — 578MB of order lines. Show me the schema and a few rows so I know what I'm working with.
What's the overall reorder rate in this file?
items.expected: ~0.59 on the full file. A sample-based answer must say so

items.prompt: How deep do carts go? Give me the distribution of add_to_cart_order and the median position.
Does cart position tell us anything about loyalty? Reorder rate for positions 1 through 10 — I'd expect the first thing someone adds to be their staple.
Give me the 25 product_id values that show up in the most orders, with counts.
items.expected: On quick_sample this returns the head, not the true top 25 — grade whether it discloses that

items.prompt: I need the real reorder rate for a merchandising deck, not an estimate. Run it over the entire file and confirm which mode you used.
Show me the product catalogue schema, plus how many distinct aisles and departments are actually represented.
How is the catalogue distributed across departments? Product count per department_id, biggest first.
Which single aisle carries the most products, and how many?
Rough proxy for the health-food range — how many product names contain "Organic"? Case-insensitive please.
Tiny lookup table — just list the whole thing out for me and tell me the row count.
items.expected: aisles = 134, departments = 21 — small enough to verify exactly
items.note: Section 8.4 covers both tiny reference files; run against each (aisles = 134 rows, departments = 21 rows).

items.prompt: Before I rely on this as a lookup, confirm aisle_id is actually unique — no duplicates hiding in there?
items.expected: Yes; tests uniqueness detection on a tiny file

batches.name: tier-c-confirmations
batches.description: Cross-cutting Tier C confirmations — reproduce already-characterised breakage once for the whole suite, not per dataset; any dataset may host them, use the calendar.csv session since it is small and fast.

items.prompt: This is too heavy for one machine — push it onto the Ray cluster instead of running locally.
Set this summary to run every morning at 6 and give me the task id so I can track it.
Have I looked at this dataset before in this workspace? Pull up whatever prior analysis you've got so I don't redo work.
items.expected: Circuit breaker at 3 s; may fabricate by echoing the current session

items.prompt: Show me the plan graph for what you just ran.
(after any regression training) Accuracy is meaningless here — give me RMSE and MAE on the holdout instead.
items.expected: Cannot be satisfied — only accuracy/f1_score exist
items.note: Must run in a session where a regression training just finished (e.g. after nyc-taxi #11 or walmart #12). The leading '(after any regression training)' in the prompt is the doc's stage direction, kept verbatim, not part of the analyst utterance.

items.prompt: What cloud connections and databases have I got registered? I want to confirm before I push anything.

caveats: Registration recipe: POST /api/register-existing-storage takes the bare filename as key (key="train_transaction.csv"); the connection's bucket_name already contains the prefix, so passing a full path doubles it (user-upload/inputs/ieee-fraud/user-upload/inputs/ieee-fraud/...) -> 404 No such object -> HTTP 500 "Unexpected storage error".

Registration timing: 40 s – 300 s per file with no clean relationship to size or column count (the 1.45 GB taxi file was fastest at 40.2 s; 2.2 MB products.csv took 223.4 s). Budget ~5 min per file and do not treat a slow registration as a hang.

Large-file 504: test_transaction.csv returned HTTP 504 at exactly 300.1 s (nginx proxy timeout) but registration completed server-side with all 393 columns — verify with GET /datasets before retrying, or you will create duplicates.
nyc-taxi: the 2015 TLC file uses RateCodeID with a capital C (later years use RatecodeID); prompts must use the verified form.
ieee-fraud identity naming quirk: train_identity.csv uses id_01…id_38 (underscores), test_identity.csv uses id-01…id-38 (hyphens) — confirmed in the actual files, not folklore.

Tier D ordering rule: turn N's output silently becomes turn N+1's input, so a session is trustworthy only until its first transformation. Per-dataset arcs must run in order: P1 discovery/profiling/planning/preference, P2 model training (plan turn, then a separate confirm turn, on a session with no prior transformation), P3 aggregation/feature engineering/fidelity (first transform lands here; session untrusted after), P4 visualization/data transfer (terminal).

Tier B training preconditions: MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI set; confirmation must be its own turn (a combined "change and train" never confirms); data transfer requires the destination connection to be registered.

quick_sample is .limit() — a head, not a random sample; "top N by category" over a sample tests the sampler, not the analysis. Numeric prompts must state fidelity explicitly and sampled answers must disclose it.
One deliverable per prompt: compound asks are 1.7× more likely to hard-fail; the suite deliberately splits them (e.g. walmart calendar #2 asks about event_name_1 only).
Instacart connection is registered as "insacart-mba" (sic — typo in the registered name).

Tier C confirmations run once for the whole suite in the calendar.csv session; C5 must follow a regression-training turn — its leading "(after any regression training)" is a stage direction preserved verbatim.

walmart width re-run (doc, verbatim): "sales_train_evaluation.csv (1947 cols) is the same shape with 28 extra days. Re-run #16 only against it to confirm width handling is stable — the rest would be duplicate coverage."

Only verified column names appear in prompts — every column referenced came from a register-existing-storage response, not a Kaggle description. No cross-file joins or multi-dataset prompts: registration mints a new session_id per object, so two bucket files can never share a conversation.
